html:
The Jarawara are a small Indigenous people of the Purus River region in Amazonas, Brazil. They speak a dialect of Madí, an Arawá language shared with the Jamamadi and the Banawá.

They live in a few villages in the forest, hunting, fishing and farming. Their language is well known to linguists through the work of R. M. W. Dixon, who described its unusual grammar of gender and tense. Rubber tappers entered the region from the late 1800s. Their neighbours include the Suruwahá.
